newsitem.title: UK: Licht sees lower world sugar prices in 1996/97.
newsitem.headline: Licht sees lower world sugar prices in 1996/97.

text.p: World sugar stocks are expected to rise again in the 1996/97 crop year and depress world market prices, German statistician F.O. Licht said in its first estimate of 1996/97 production, released on Monday.

"Even if demand should grow at the same fast pace as last year, and taking into account unrecorded consumption, this estimate points to another addition to world sugar stocks and lower world market prices," Licht said.
The report pegged world sugar output at 126.61 million tonnes raw value in the 1996/97 crop year, 3.55 million higher than in 1995/96.
It gave no estimate of the level of stocks expected in 1996/97.

With production increases expected in major exporters Brazil, Thailand, South Africa and Australia, world raw sugar supplies would be abundant in 1996/97 especially if the Cuban crop maintained its upward path of recovery.
But some of the increase would be absorbed by higher U.S. import demand, it added.

Licht said the situation in the white sugar sector appeared more critical as output in the European Union (EU) and India was expected to fall, while Russian demand could rise given this year's unsatisfactory crop and fall in Ukrainian production.
But India's trading position on the world market would remain unaffected by the lower forecast because of its already high stocks, it said.
It added that the local sugar industry was already lobbying the government to release two million tonnes for export after the one million tonnes allowed last season.
"This means that supplies of low quality whites may rise in spite of lower production," the report said.

"The fall in EU production is not pronounced enough to have any material impact on exports and the total shipped could be even higher than last season, depending on the carry-over of C sugar to 1997/98," it added.
Hopes for higher Russian demand could prove illusory given the government's efforts to curb imports to support the domestic sugar industry and the lack of foreign currency.
"White sugar demand could fall given higher production in Turkey, lower requirements from the Near and Middle East and greater competition from countries such as Brazil," Licht said.
"This reveals that the situation is rather complex and that the slow down in production growth need not necessarily mean stable world market prices."
